subject: English
description: Meanings of common and less-common phrasal verbs

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of the phrasal verb in: 'The manager decided to put off the meeting until next week.'

options.option_text: Cancel
Postpone
Attend
Prepare for

questions.explanation: 'Put off' = to postpone or delay something. Cancel = call off or drop entirely. Common confusable — 'put on' (wear clothes / gain weight / stage a show), 'put out' (extinguish a fire / publish a statement), 'put up with' (tolerate).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of 'look down upon' in: 'She looks down upon people who don't share her opinions.'

options.option_text: Examine closely
Regard with contempt
Guide or mentor
Be friendly with

questions.explanation: 'Look down upon' = to regard someone as inferior; to despise. Opposite — 'look up to' = to respect or admire. Related — 'look after' (take care of), 'look into' (investigate), 'look over' (inspect briefly), 'look forward to' (anticipate with pleasure).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of 'bring about' in: 'The new policy has brought about a significant change.'

options.option_text: Cancel
Cause to happen
Delay
Reject

questions.explanation: 'Bring about' = to cause something to happen. Synonyms — cause, effect, produce, result in. Related — 'bring up' (raise a child OR introduce a topic), 'bring on' (cause something negative), 'bring in' (introduce / yield revenue), 'bring out' (reveal / publish).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of 'cut down on' in: 'I need to cut down on my sugar intake.'

options.option_text: Increase
Reduce
Replace entirely
Measure precisely

questions.explanation: 'Cut down on' = reduce the quantity of something. Stronger — 'cut out' = eliminate entirely (cut out sugar). Related — 'cut off' (stop abruptly / disconnect), 'cut in' (interrupt / join a queue ahead of others), 'cut back' (reduce — similar to cut down, used for services / spending).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of 'break down' in: 'His car broke down on the highway.'

options.option_text: Accelerated
Stopped working
Turned around
Was repaired

questions.explanation: 'Break down' (of a machine) = stop functioning. Other senses — (of a person) lose emotional control and cry; (of a substance) decompose chemically. Related — 'break up' (end a relationship / disperse a crowd), 'break out' (start suddenly — war, disease, fire), 'break in' (enter forcibly / interrupt / wear new shoes).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of 'carry out' in: 'The scientists will carry out further tests before releasing the drug.'

options.option_text: Transport
Perform or execute
Suspend
Advertise

questions.explanation: 'Carry out' = perform, execute, complete (a task, order, plan, experiment). Trap — 'carry' literally means 'to take', so students misread this as 'transport'. Related — 'carry on' (continue), 'carry off' (succeed in something difficult; also, take away as a prize or victim), 'carry over' (extend into a new period — leave days, balance).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of 'fall out with' in: 'He fell out with his best friend over a trivial matter.'

options.option_text: Fell physically
Quarrelled and stopped being friends
Went on a trip together
Helped out

questions.explanation: 'Fall out (with)' = have a serious disagreement that damages the relationship. Related fall- phrasals — 'fall through' (a plan failing), 'fall for' (be deceived by / fall in love with), 'fall back on' (rely on when other options fail), 'fall behind' (lag).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: What does the phrasal verb 'give up' mean in: 'Despite repeated failures, she refused to give up her dream of becoming a doctor'?

options.option_text: To hand over something to a higher authority
To abandon or stop trying to achieve a goal
To postpone a decision for a much later date
To sacrifice something valuable for another person

questions.explanation: B is correct because 'give up' means to cease trying or to relinquish an effort entirely — she refuses to stop pursuing her dream despite setbacks. Option D ('sacrifice for another person') is a common distractor but 'give up' here denotes abandoning one's own effort, not a selfless act for others.

questions.stem: What does 'take after' mean in: 'Everyone says Riya takes after her grandmother in both looks and temperament'?

options.option_text: To imitate someone's behaviour in a calculated way
To physically follow a person from place to place
To look after an elderly relative with great care
To resemble a family member in looks or character

questions.explanation: D is correct because 'take after' means to have a natural resemblance to a parent or ancestor in appearance or personality. Option A ('imitate') is the most tempting distractor — but 'imitate' implies deliberate copying, whereas 'take after' refers to an inherited, not intentional, likeness.

questions.stem: In which sentence is the phrasal verb 'set off' used to mean 'to trigger or cause something to begin suddenly'?

options.option_text: The hikers set off at dawn to reach the summit by noon
The jewellery set off her traditional silk saree beautifully
The vibration set off the fire alarm in the corridor
The dark frame helped set off the portrait from the background

questions.explanation: C is correct — 'set off' here means to activate or trigger the alarm. Option A is a common error: 'set off' in option A means 'to begin a journey', which is the everyday usage most candidates know. Option B uses 'set off' meaning 'to enhance or complement', used in aesthetic contexts.

questions.stem: What does 'run into' mean in: 'While waiting at the railway station, he ran into his former professor from university'?

options.option_text: To chase someone who is moving quickly away from you
To meet or encounter someone by chance unexpectedly
To collide with a person while rushing in a hurry
To face a serious obstacle while completing a task

questions.explanation: B is correct because 'run into' idiomatically means to meet someone by accident. Option C ('collide with') represents the most frequent wrong answer — candidates interpret 'run into' literally (physical collision), missing the idiomatic meaning. Option D applies when 'run into' is followed by difficulties, not a person.

questions.stem: Which phrasal verb best completes the sentence: 'Against all odds, the small local team managed to _____ a stunning victory in the national finals'?

options.option_text: pull out — withdraw suddenly from an agreed situation
pull through — recover from a very difficult setback
pull apart — separate competing elements by force
pull off — succeed in something despite the challenges

questions.explanation: D is correct because 'pull off' means to accomplish something difficult or improbable against expectations — exactly what the team did. Option B ('pull through') is the strongest distractor: it relates to overcoming adversity, but specifically means recovering from illness or crisis, not achieving a triumph.

questions.stem: In which sentence is 'see through' used to mean 'to perceive the hidden truth behind something deceptive'?

options.option_text: The glass door allowed us to see through to the garden
The shrewd detective could see through the criminal's false alibi
She promised to see through the renovation project to completion
He held the film negative up to see through it clearly

questions.explanation: B is correct — 'see through' means to detect or expose a lie or deception; the detective recognised the alibi was fabricated. Option C is the trickiest distractor: it uses 'see through' to mean 'continue a task until the end' (another legitimate meaning). Options A and D use 'see through' in its literal physical sense (optical transparency).

questions.stem: In which sentence is the phrasal verb 'make out' used specifically to mean 'to decipher or understand something with difficulty'?

options.option_text: He tried to make out that he was unaware of the entire incident
Despite the blurred handwriting, she could make out the address
The couple could be seen making out near the old banyan tree
How did the new employees make out in their first performance review?

questions.explanation: B is correct — 'make out' here means to read or understand something that is obscure or unclear. Option A ('make out that') means to falsely claim or pretend, which is equally standard and confuses many candidates. Option D uses informal American English where 'make out' means to fare or manage, and option C uses the informal meaning of being romantically intimate.
